catalog_quote: [p. 1034] § 4. Fonology. The fonetics of Chontal present very little difficulty for a European. There is no pitch tone. The stress accent is placed almost invariably on the last syllable. This is especially noticeable in words borrowed from the Spanish, where those words in Spanish carry the stress on the penultima. To a Spanish ear this comes as a shock. ... [p. 1040] 2. Grammatical Processes. ... b) Reduplication is absent. c) Accentual differences are absent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the word ('almost invariably'); the language has no pitch tone; stress is not exploited as a grammatical process (no accentual alternations). Spanish loanwords with penultimate stress in Spanish are re-stressed on the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'almost invariably'; no specific exceptions listed. The 'accentual differences are absent' remark (p. 1040) refers to Sapir-style grammatical processes, i.e. stress shift is not used morphologically (contrast Highland Chontal, where Turner reports plural by stress shift).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('the stress accent' of the word; illustrated by loanwords); based on 1920s field material from Tequixistlan (Tequisistlan), texts plus vocabulary. Belmar 1900 (variety unstated) instead says stress is invariably on the principal root with each syllable keeping its own accent, felt especially word-finally -- noted, not adopted, because its dialect identity is uncertain.
new_statements.identity_note: de Angulo & Freeland's data are from Tequixistlan (Tequisistlan), 'the most important Chontal town' (p. 1033), i.e. the extinct third Oaxaca Chontal variety that Glottolog lists as tequ1245 'Tequistlateco Chontal' (its Glottolog's most extensive description is exactly this 1925 sketch). Maddieson, Avelino & O'Connor 2009: 70 (citing Waterhouse 1985) say this variety was closer to Lowland Chontal (lowl1260, where Waterhouse & Morrison 1950 report contrastive stress) than to Highland Chontal (high1242, default penultimate per Turner). Belmar 1900 names no locality; de Angulo & Freeland (p. 1033) suspect a different dialect from theirs, and Maddieson et al. treat it as Highland -- so Belmar's 'acento en la raíz principal' statement is recorded but not attributed to tequ1245. Note the 'Tequistlateco/Tequistlatec' label is also used in the literature (Oltrogge 1977; Turner & Turner 1971) for the Highland variety, which is NOT this languoid.
